section_1.title: Prerequisite: The Binary vs. The Wave
section_1.content: Transition from classical bits (0 or 1) to the wave-like nature of quantum mechanics. Introduce the concept that quantum systems exist as probability waves until measured.
section_1.example: Comparing a light switch (On/Off) with a spinning coin (blurred state of both).

section_2.title: Defining Superposition
section_2.content: Explain superposition mathematically as a linear combination of basis states: |ψ⟩ = α|0⟩ + β|1⟩. Emphasize that α and β are probability amplitudes, not probabilities themselves.
section_2.example: Visualizing two ripples in a pond overlapping; the height at any point is the sum of the two wave amplitudes.

section_3.title: The Measurement Problem
section_3.content: Explain the 'Collapse of the Wavefunction.' When we interact with the system, the superposition collapses into a single definite state based on |α|² and |β|².
section_3.example: Schrödinger’s Cat: The cat is represented by a wave function |Alive⟩ + |Dead⟩. Opening the box (measurement) forces the system into |Alive⟩ or |Dead⟩.

section_4.title: Visualizing Quantum States (Bloch Sphere)
section_4.content: Introduce the Bloch Sphere as a geometric representation of a qubit. Show how a state vector can point anywhere on the surface, representing unique superpositions of |0⟩ and |1⟩.
section_4.example: A compass needle that can point to 'North' (0), 'South' (1), or any point on the globe, representing different ratios of 0 and 1.

section_5.title: Real-World Application: Quantum Computing
section_5.content: Briefly summarize how superposition allows quantum computers to process multiple possibilities simultaneously, providing exponential speedups for specific algorithms.
section_5.example: A quantum 'maze solver' that explores all paths of a labyrinth at once, rather than trying one turn at a time like a classical mouse.
